item.title: 🔵 Secure your AI estate: 5 things CIOs must know about AI agents
item.description:
Why this matters: Potential data exposure — review monitoring and incident-response readiness.

What CIOs need to know about AI agents

Enterprise AI adoption is entering a new phase. Generative AI gave employees new ways to create content and access information, primarily through AI web applications. Embedded AI copilots began helping them work natively in existing applications.

Now, AI agents are running locally on employee workstations, with expansive user permissions, and are increasingly capable of autonomously executing work.

An AI agent is an LLM-powered software system that can reason over context, make decisions, and pursue an objective with a degree of autonomy. Unlike conventional software built around predefined logic, agents introduce probabilistic, context-sensitive reasoning into how tasks are interpreted and executed. They can interpret changing inputs, determine what to do next, use tools and enterprise systems, and adapt as a task unfolds.

item.title: 🔵 What a cockatoo can teach us about the evidence AI wasn’t built to hear
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

AI systems do not make decisions from reality. They make decisions from representations of reality: records, observations, measurements, histories, labels, documents, and whatever else an organization has decided belongs in the data. That distinction sounds almost too obvious to be interesting, yet it becomes surprisingly easy to forget once an AI system can process thousands of records, identify patterns no person would notice, and return an answer that appears comprehensive. The sophistication of the analysis can distract us from a more basic problem: important information may never enter the decision process in a form the system can use.

Much of the responsible-AI conversation begins after that problem has already occurred. We ask whether a model is accurate, whether its recommendation can be explained, whether a human remains involved, and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Those are necessary questions, but they assume that the relevant evidence made it into the decision somewhere. They’ve built CI/CD pipelines, elaborate test suites, code repositories, and tools galore, all with the goal of keeping the systems up and running.

Now AI is throwing a wrench into the whole endeavor. Software is now more complex and sometimes mysteriously unpredictable. Expectations are sky high, but no one is certain what to expect in good conscience.

Luckily, dozens of companies are rushing to build new tools designed to keep agentic stacks on the straight and narrow, delivering value to everyone. The field is rapidly evolving, probably having changed since you started reading this article.

Some of the tools involved in the emerging agent stack aren’t that different from what enterprise teams already have in store. item.title: 🟠 MCP is changing the questions marketers can afford to ask
item.description:

Picture a regional marketing director on a Monday morning. She’s got 80 locations, a cup of coffee, and a nagging feeling that something is off in the Southeast. Reviews seem quieter. A couple of stores got new managers last month. Are those two things related?

Not long ago, finding out meant pulling an export, building a pivot table, pulling a second export from another system, and stitching it all together in a spreadsheet. Or, more realistically, filing a request with an analyst and waiting. Most weeks, the question simply never got asked.

item.title: 🔵 Human in the loop is an engineering problem
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

A customer leaves a one-star review at one of your locations. An AI drafts a reply in seconds. It’s warm, on-brand, grammatically perfect, and it thanks the customer for their feedback and invites them back soon.

The review was about a customer who slipped and was hurt in the parking lot.

Nothing in that reply is factually false. It would pass a spell-checker, a brand-voice check, and probably a quick skim from a busy manager. It’s still the wrong answer, and if it goes out publicly, it’s the kind of wrong that ends up in a screenshot.

I spend most of my time building systems that put AI to work on reputation data: reviews, listings, surveys, and the replies and summaries generated from them. The most important lesson I’ve learned is that “human in the loop” is an engineering problem. Where the human sits, what they see, what gets routed to them and what doesn’t—all of that is system design.

item.description:

Enterprises have historically built separate network and security architectures, but this separation is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain as frontier AI models mature and security architectures shift from perimeter-based defenses to identity- and context-aware enforcement.

Frontier AI does not change existing cybersecurity fundamentals; it narrows the time available to apply them. As attacks move from human speed to machine speed, enterprises need security controls that can detect, respond, and enforce at the same speed. The network is uniquely positioned to become that enforcement and containment fabric.

The AI era requires enterprises to treat the network as an active security control, not simply as infrastructure to be protected. By integrating identity, telemetry, segmentation, and automated enforcement, the network can reduce exposure, contain compromise, and accelerate recovery at machine speed.

item.title: 🟠 Unplug your smart fridges, French supermarkets warned after cyberattack
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

More internet-connected refrigerators have joined the official list of those affected by a cyberattack that ruined stocks of chilled food at hundreds of French supermarkets over the weekend.

The French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) advised supermarkets to disconnect any refrigeration control systems with a public IP address from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults.

In an emergency, it suggested, they could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution, CERT-FR said.

CERT-FR’s initial warning on Monday listed only Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series refrigeration controllers as affected, advising supermarkets to update the firmware of their systems, set the security level to “strict,” and ensure that default passwords had been changed.

But for CIOs, that comes with a risk: if the technology gives customers the wrong information, makes biased recommendations, or mishandles data, it can immediately damage the trust companies have worked hard to build.

Unlike conventional software, gen AI doesn’t always give the same answer to the same question. An answer can sound confident and convincing while still wrong. And when customers rely on AI for information about their finances, insurance, or health, a mistake can have much greater consequences.

item.title: 🟠 AI is changing (and chaining) the cybersecurity math
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

For years, cybersecurity teams have worked from a relatively straightforward model: identify the critical vulnerability, patch it and reduce the risk.  That model still matters, but it is no longer enough.

The growing concern is not simply that attackers can use AI to write better phishing emails or generate malicious code faster. The bigger issue is that AI can help adversaries connect seemingly benign vulnerabilities into an attack path that security teams may never have considered.

A low-severity application flaw, exposed API, over-permissioned service account, cloud misconfiguration and AI agent with excessive access may not be alarming individually. But when they can be identified, sequenced and exploited together, they can create a serious breach.

This is the new cybersecurity challenge: AI-enabled vulnerability service chaining.

item.title: 🔴 Cybersecurity is a leadership problem: Why the management model needs to catch up
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

When I started writing regularly about cybersecurity management in 2015, the environment looked very different.

Cloud computing was still reshaping enterprise technology. Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions. Zero Trust had yet to enter mainstream technical vocabulary and quantum computing barely registered on the corporate risk horizon.

Cybersecurity itself also occupied a different position. The CISO role was less established, board engagement was inconsistent, regulation was less extensive and security budgets were generally smaller.

Much has changed since then.

But looking back at the management challenges we were discussing more than a decade ago raises an uncomfortable question:

Why are we still discussing so many of them?

item.description:

There’s growing talk of digital sovereignty as enterprises rethink past consolidation decisions made in the name of simplicity.

Mozilla, developer of Firefox, argues that a “very specific, very important layer” has been mostly missing from that conversation: The browser.

To that end, the company has unveiled Firefox Enterprise in a bid to diversify the browser engine to support privacy, control, and security.

item.title: 🟠 Over 1,500 npm packages exposed by Trusted Publishing validation flaw
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

A flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing mechanism could allow attackers to hijack legitimate software packages by reclaiming abandoned GitHub repository names, potentially exposing millions of package downloads to supply-chain attacks.

Researchers at Bloom Security identified more than 1500 potentially vulnerable npm packages, including security scanners, authentication tools, and cryptographic packages.

The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned.

The issue is now fixed, Bloom Security researcher Golan Myers told CSO. “The npm team confirmed that a fix had been shipped on October 2, introducing a 48-hour expiry for unvalidated Trusted Publishin…

item.title: 🟠 These ARE the droids you’re looking for
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

There’s an old leadership fantasy that goes something like this: The CISO surveys a sprawling technology estate, discovers 11 tools doing the work of four, calculates the licensing savings, selects a shiny new strategic platform and declares that consolidation has begun. Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12.

I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies. At CME Group, I eventually gave myself an unofficial title: chief decommissioning officer. The job was considerably less glamorous than the acronym suggested. I had to find technology that had overstayed its welcome, identify who believed they still owned it, determine who actually depended on it and, occasionally, put a bullet in its head.

Buying technology is easy. Killing technology is hard. Tool sprawl is rarely just a technology problem but rather an organizational psychology problem. The industry’s solution has traditionally been consolidation. Buy a platform. Standardize the stack. Reduce vendors and centralize procurement…

item.title: 🔴 Researchers bypass 6 AI agent frameworks with a simple ‘Repeat-After-Me’ prompt
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Researchers have tricked six widely used AI agent frameworks into running tool calls written by an attacker, simply by asking the underlying model to repeat the call back.

The technique, which the researchers call “Repeat-After-Me,” worked on LangChain’s LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft’s AutoGen, Google’s Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS’ Strands Agents and CrewAI, according to researchers from Pennsylvania State University, Université Montpellier and Dartmouth College.

“A seemingly benign text-repetition request thus gives the attacker direct control over the tool invocation and its arguments,” the researchers wrote in the paper.

The same paper reports that a testing tool the team built found verified security bugs in 118 of the 273 open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it was able to run.

Lightwell, the open-source security initiative set up by IBM and Red Hat, has identified more than 400 previously undiscovered vulnerabilities in widely used Java libraries — and now the companies are inviting customers to submit their own code dependencies to a new service, Lightwell Clearinghouse, for review.

They’ll be looking for bugs such as the critical sandbox bypass in Java template engine Thymeleaf, with a CVSS score of 9.1, discovered in April.
